title: Nicéphore Niépce made it sometime between 1822 and 1827, using a process he called heliography, mean
description:
Nicéphore Niépce made it sometime between 1822 and 1827, using a process he called heliography, meaning sun-drawing. Historians narrowed the window from his letters to his brother; nobody has pinned it closer than that.

The popular version says the exposure took eight hours. That number is a mid-twentieth-century guess, based only on how sunlight falls on both sides of the buildings in the image. A researcher who rebuilt Niépce's process using historically accurate materials found it actually needed several days of exposure, not hours.

photography historians who tracked down Niépce's photograph after it had effectively vanished from view earlier in the twentieth century.

Niépce partnered with Louis Daguerre in 1829. After Niépce died in 1833, Daguerre kept working alone and unveiled his own process a decade later, naming it after himself. The French government paid Daguerre 6,000 francs a year for it. Niépce's own estate received only 4,000.

The man who actually took photography's first surviving picture died broke. His grave was paid for by his town.
